comparison: Perfect alignment on background claims (C1-C2, C12-C19). Both evaluations support these as established context and prior knowledge without challenge. OpenEval emphasizes the rationale for CCR2-DTR mice, while peer reviewers accept the framing without question.

Strong agreement on MHC II transfer experiments (C5-C7, C38-C40, C52, C64). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs do not directly prime T cells but transfer antigen to cDCs. Peer reviewers describe this as a 'major conclusion' accepted without challenge, while OpenEval notes the logic is 'internally consistent and well-controlled.'

Strong agreement on cDC requirement for T cell priming (C8-C9, C41-C47). Both evaluations support the dissociation between bacterial transport (maintained) and T cell priming (impaired) when cDCs are depleted. Peer reviewers accept this as part of understanding 'different APCs in transport and presentation,' while OpenEval emphasizes convergent results from independent genetic systems.

Strong agreement on IM depletion experiments (C3-C4, C21-C27). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs are required for bacterial transport and T cell priming. Peer reviewers describe the study as 'elegant and straightforward' and accept the core finding, while OpenEval notes 'converging evidence' from multiple experimental readouts. Peer review also includes C48-C49 in this grouping.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty regarding antigen transfer mechanism (C61-C63). Both evaluations mark this as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers explicitly identify this as 'the only open aspect' and request mechanistic insights, while OpenEval notes the mechanism 'remains speculative and requires future investigation.' Both acknowledge C64's conclusion about minimal MHC transfer role.

Partial overlap on IM adoptive transfer experiments (C29-C35). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the rigorous purification strategy and functional rescue of both transport and priming, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology by describing the study as 'elegant' without raising concerns. Peer review groups these with C10-C11, C50.

Partial overlap on the integrated model (C10-C11, C50). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs and cDCs perform distinct but complementary functions. OpenEval synthesizes this as 'the central mechanistic insight,' while peer reviewers accept it as part of the overall contribution. Peer review also includes adoptive transfer claims (C32-C35) in this grouping.

Partial overlap on CCR2 independence for trafficking (C36-C37). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the direct comparison showing CCR2 is dispensable for lung-to-lymph node trafficking, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their validation of methodological controls. Peer review also includes purification strategy claims (C29-C31) in this grouping.

Partial overlap on methodological details (C29-C31). Both evaluations support the rigorous IM purification strategy. OpenEval provides detailed validation noting >99% purity and addresses confounding from other CCR2+ cells (C20, C28, C68-C71), while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology without questioning the purification approach.

Minimal overlap (C56 only). OpenEval evaluates C51, C53-C59 as SUPPORTED background literature providing context for interpreting findings. Peer review R5 focuses on the unresolved mechanism (C56, C61-C63) and marks it UNCERTAIN. The evaluations address different aspects with little substantive overlap.

OpenEval evaluates zDC-DTR mouse model characteristics (C65-C67) as SUPPORTED background with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these methodological background claims.
